newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russia analysts look for productivity and openness.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russia analysts look for productivity and openness.

text.p: Investors in Russian equities should ignore traditional financial indicators and focus on a company's productivity and openness to investors to find a good buy, according to equity analysts in this opaque but booming market.
The Russian Trading System Index of leading shares has risen almost 45 percent since the beginning of the year, but many of the companies are poorly known and produce poor quality data.

"If you do not know how much cash a company generates, at least you can understand how much oil it has control over, and you can price shares per tonne of oil, or kilowatt hour," said Christopher Smart, director of research at the Pioneer First Investment Group in Moscow.
"We look at underlying assets in terms of barrels of oil or number of telephone lines."
Russian government statistics put national telephone ownership at 18 lines per 100 people, compared with 56 in the United States and 40 in Western Europe, a sound indication of growth potential.

But Smart said that Russian accounts, prepared to satisfy tax authorities than to make investment decisions, were useful chiefly as a way of looking at a single company's performance growth over a number of years.
Analysts say that the accounts need major reworking to give even a basic indication of a company's financial standing.
"Russian accounts are really hard to work with," said Jim Nail, head of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Moscow.
"Russian standard price earnings ratios are basically useless, even comparing companies to one another within Russia, and even within the same sector."
Even major companies typically have less than three years' worth of Western-style accounts.
Nail said price-sales ratios were probably the most objective numbers to use when analysing companies, but even those often include overvalued barter "sales".

The Russian oil sector has an unweighted price sales ratio of about 0.75, at least one third that of Western competitors, he said, while telecoms have an unweighted p/s ratio of about 1.75 versus 2.5 in Latin America.
COMPANIES PROVIDING INFORMATION WORTH A PREMIUM

But Russian companies, many still oriented towards a Soviet command-style economy and unfamiliar with raising and using investment funds or making a profit, could also be ranked by their openness to the West, analysts say.

"The market is rewarding companies that are open and punishing those that are not," said Smart. "That's why you get the market cap of (oil company) LUKoil outpacing (natural gas monopoly and Russia's largest company,) Gazprom."
Mark Maurer, a partner at Ernst & Young in Moscow, said companies seeking Western audits often produced the soundest investment information and had the best potential.
"Data reliability is improving in companies that have Western investment and Western managers," he said, but he warned that openness to Western ideas did not guarantee sound figures.

"We prefer to use a company's production figures, but the important thing is to understand the basis for the statistics," Maurer said. "You can use any statistic you want, but you have to know what they mean."
Official Russian figures for oil exports can differ by hundreds of thousands of tonnes. But Maurer said such figures could be useful if the calculation methodology was clear.
INVESTORS LOOK FOR UNDERVALUATION OR GROWTH POTENTIAL
Russian companies offer two different reasons for investment -- earnings growth and undervaluation -- championed by different analysts.

A company's share price should rise with its earnings, analysts say, but a sudden flurry of interest in an unknown firm could force a re-evaluation of its share price and bring quicker returns, some argue.
Nail said growth potential was a better basis for investment since analysts could broadly predict a company's performance.
"A lot of growth estimates depend on your view of macroeconomic tendencies," Nail said. "But you can make some more or less reasonable assumptions about broad trends if you don't pin a date on them."
Investors who have poured funds into the Russian shares market often expect Russian economic growth only in 1998.
Gross domestic product shrank by six percent in 1996 and many officials doubt forecasts of two percent growth this year.
Nail calculated Russian utilities would succeed, based on rising income and higher household electricity rates, which would put Russia more in line with other emerging economies.
Russian utilities have price-sales ratios close to utilities in Britain, but growth potential was enormous in Russia and low in Britain, he said.
Investors expecting to reap a windfall on re-evaluation could wait a long time for the market, hindered by a lack of information, to send share prices soaring.
Smart said growth potential was a good reason to invest but added that the process of researching a company stimulated the market's re-evaluation process.
"There are still a great many companies that are underpriced simply because people haven't focused attention on them."
